decks.title: Microbes in Human Welfare — Part 1: Microbes at home and in industry
goals: Explain the role of Lactobacillus, Saccharomyces and Propionibacterium in household products
Name microbes used to make beverages, antibiotics, organic acids, alcohol and enzymes
State the sources and uses of streptokinase, cyclosporin A and statins

slides.heading: Useful microbes
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the bacteria and fungi that make our curd, bread and cheese, and the medicines and chemicals of industry.

visual.alt: Flow from household uses to industrial fermentation to medicines and enzymes

slides.narration: Not all microbes cause disease. Many are used every day, in our kitchens and in large factories, to make food, drinks, medicines and chemicals.

slides.heading: Microbes in household products
slides.body_md: Fermentation by microbes changes the taste, texture and nutritive value of food.

rows: Makes lactic acid that coagulates and partly digests milk proteins; adds vitamin B12
Ferments sugar in dough; carbon dioxide makes it rise
Fermentation; carbon dioxide puffs the batter

visual.alt: Table of household products and the microbes that make them

slides.narration: A spoonful of curd added to warm milk supplies lactic acid bacteria that turn the milk into curd. Yeast makes bread rise, and a bacterium called Propionibacterium makes the large holes in Swiss cheese.

slides.heading: How milk becomes curd
slides.body_md: **Lactobacillus** and other **lactic acid bacteria (LAB)** multiply in warm milk and make **lactic acid**. The **pH falls** from about 6.57 to about 4.41, and milk proteins **coagulate**.

slides.narration: At first little changes, then the acid builds up quickly as the bacteria multiply, and finally the curve levels off when the curd has set. In the stomach, lactic acid bacteria also help to check disease-causing microbes.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: multiplying lactic acid bacteria
slides.body_md: A starter adds about 1000 lactic acid bacteria per millilitre to warm milk. If they double every 1 hour, how many are there per millilitre after 6 hours?
bullets: Number of doublings $= \dfrac{6}{1} = 6$.
Bacteria $= 1000 \times 2^{6} = 64000$ per millilitre.
This rapid growth explains the steep fall in pH in the middle of the curve.

visual.alt: Worked table: 64000 bacteria per millilitre after 6 hours

slides.narration: Six doublings multiply the number sixty four times. As the bacteria multiply, they make more and more lactic acid, so the milk sets within a few hours in a warm place but much more slowly in the cold.

slides.heading: Quick check: cheese
slides.body_md: Which microbe makes the large holes in Swiss cheese?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is a bacterium that releases a gas.

slides.heading: Fermented beverages
slides.body_md: **Saccharomyces cerevisiae** (**brewer’s yeast**) ferments **malted cereals and fruit juices** to make ethanol.

visual.alt: Table of beverages and whether they are distilled

slides.narration: Wine and beer are made by fermentation alone. Whisky, brandy and rum are distilled after fermentation, which concentrates the alcohol. The same yeast is used in industry to make ethanol for fuel and chemicals.

slides.heading: Antibiotics: the story of penicillin
slides.body_md: **Antibiotics** are chemicals produced by some microbes that **kill or retard the growth** of other, disease-causing microbes. **Alexander Fleming** noticed that a mould, **Penicillium notatum**, growing on a culture of **Staphylococcus** stopped the bacteria growing around it. **Ernst Chain and Howard Florey** later established its full potential.

rows: Treated wounded soldiers in World War II; reduced deaths from plague, whooping cough, diphtheria and leprosy

visual.alt: Table about the discovery of penicillin

slides.narration: A chance contamination led to the first antibiotic. Penicillin saved many lives in the Second World War, and antibiotics have since greatly reduced deaths from bacterial diseases.

slides.heading: Organic acids, alcohol and enzymes
slides.body_md: Microbes are grown in large vessels to produce useful chemicals.

visual.alt: Table of organic acids, alcohol and enzymes with microbes and uses

slides.narration: Fungi such as Aspergillus and bacteria such as Acetobacter are grown in bulk to make acids for food. Lipases in detergents digest oily stains, and pectinases and proteases make bottled juices clear.

slides.heading: Bioactive molecules for medicine
slides.body_md: Some microbial products act directly on the human body.

rows: “Clot buster”: removes clots in blood vessels of heart-attack patients
Lower blood cholesterol by competitively inhibiting the enzyme of cholesterol synthesis

visual.alt: Table of bioactive molecules with microbes and uses

slides.narration: Streptokinase dissolves clots in patients who have had a heart attack. Cyclosporin A suppresses the immune system so that a transplanted organ is not rejected. Statins compete with the enzyme that makes cholesterol and so lower its level in the blood.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: products of fermentation
slides.body_md: Yeast ferments glucose: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂ (molar masses 180, 46 and 44). What mass of ethanol and of carbon dioxide can 90 g of glucose give?
bullets: Ethanol $= 90 \times \dfrac{2 \times 46}{180} = 46$ g.
Carbon dioxide $= 90 \times \dfrac{2 \times 44}{180} = 44$ g.
The **carbon dioxide** raises bread dough; the **ethanol** is the basis of beverages and industrial alcohol.

visual.alt: Worked table: 46 g ethanol and 44 g carbon dioxide

slides.narration: Half the mass of glucose ends up as ethanol and the rest as carbon dioxide. In bread-making the gas matters and the little alcohol evaporates in baking; in brewing the alcohol matters.

slides.heading: Quick check: statins
slides.body_md: Which microbe produces statins?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is a yeast that also gives red rice its colour.

slides.heading: Quick check: penicillin
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about penicillin.
slides.narration: Quick check. Who discovered it, and who developed it into a medicine?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Household: Lactobacillus (curd, vitamin B12), Saccharomyces (bread), Propionibacterium sharmanii (Swiss cheese).
Beverages by Saccharomyces cerevisiae; distilled (whisky, brandy, rum) and undistilled (wine, beer).
Penicillin: Fleming, Penicillium notatum; Chain and Florey.
Acids: Aspergillus niger (citric), Acetobacter aceti (acetic), Clostridium butylicum (butyric), Lactobacillus (lactic).
Enzymes: lipases, pectinases, proteases, streptokinase; cyclosporin A (Trichoderma polysporum), statins (Monascus purpureus).

visual.alt: Summary table of microbes and products

slides.narration: To recap: microbes give us curd, bread and cheese at home, and drinks, antibiotics, acids, alcohol, enzymes and important medicines in industry.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Learn each product with its **microbe’s full scientific name**.
Give the **use** of streptokinase, cyclosporin A and statins.
Say which beverages are **distilled**.
Mention **vitamin B12** when explaining why curd is nutritious.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Write the full scientific name of each microbe. Learn the uses of the three medical molecules. Know which drinks are distilled. And remember that curd gains vitamin B twelve.

decks.title: Microbes in Human Welfare — Part 2: Sewage, biogas, biocontrol and biofertilisers
goals: Describe primary and secondary treatment of sewage and the meaning of BOD
Describe methanogens, the composition of biogas and the working of a biogas plant
Explain biocontrol, integrated pest management, the harm of chemical pesticides, and biofertilisers

slides.heading: Microbes for a cleaner environment
slides.body_md: Part 2 — microbes that clean sewage, make fuel, control pests and feed crops.

visual.alt: Flow from sewage treatment to biogas to biocontrol to biofertilisers

slides.narration: Cities produce huge volumes of waste water, and farms use large amounts of chemicals. Microbes can clean the water, turn waste into fuel, control pests and supply nutrients, reducing pollution.

slides.heading: Sewage treatment
slides.body_md: **Primary treatment** is physical: floating debris is removed by **filtration**, and grit and soil by **sedimentation**, leaving **primary sludge**. **Secondary (biological) treatment**: the effluent is **aerated**, and **aerobic microbes** grow as **flocs** — masses of bacteria with fungal filaments — that consume organic matter.

slides.body_md: **BOD** is the amount of **oxygen** that would be consumed if all the **organic matter** in **one litre** of water were oxidised by bacteria. The **higher the BOD**, the **more polluting** the water.

slides.narration: Secondary treatment continues until the BOD of the sewage has fallen a great deal. A low BOD shows that little organic matter remains, so the effluent will not use up the oxygen in the river it enters.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how much did treatment help?
slides.body_md: In the model plant, raw sewage has a BOD of 360 mg/L and the final effluent 24 mg/L. Find the percentage fall, and the oxygen that 5 litres of raw sewage would use.
bullets: Fall $= \dfrac{360 - 24}{360} \times 100 = 93.3$ percent.
Oxygen for 5 L of raw sewage $= 360 \times 5 = 1800$ mg.

visual.alt: Worked table: BOD falls by 93.3 percent

slides.narration: Most of the fall comes during secondary treatment, when the microbial flocs feed on organic matter. Untreated sewage would rob a river of oxygen, killing fish.

slides.heading: Methanogens and biogas
slides.body_md: **Biogas** is a mixture of gases, **mainly methane**, with **carbon dioxide** and some **hydrogen sulphide**, produced by **anaerobic** microbial activity. **Methanogens** such as **Methanobacterium** grow **anaerobically on cellulose**; they live in **anaerobic sludge** and in the **rumen of cattle**.

rows: Anaerobic sludge; rumen of cattle; cattle dung (gobar)

visual.alt: Table about methanogens and biogas

slides.narration: Bacteria in a cow’s rumen help digest the cellulose of grass, and methanogens among them produce methane. Their dung is rich in these bacteria, which is why cattle dung is the usual raw material for biogas.

slides.heading: The biogas plant
slides.body_md: A **concrete tank** (10–15 feet deep) receives a **slurry of dung**. A **floating cover** rises as gas forms; the gas is piped to houses. **Spent slurry** leaves through an outlet and is used as **fertiliser**. The technology was developed in India by **IARI** and **KVIC**.

Kill useful as well as harmful organisms

sections.heading: 1. Microbes in household products
sections.body_md:
- **Curd:** micro-organisms such as ***Lactobacillus*** and others commonly called **lactic acid bacteria (LAB)** grow in milk and convert it to curd. They produce **acids** that **coagulate and partially digest milk proteins**. A small amount of curd added to fresh milk as **inoculum (starter)** contains millions of LAB, which multiply at a suitable temperature. LAB also **improve nutritional quality** by increasing **vitamin B₁₂**, and in our stomach they help **check disease-causing microbes**.
- **Dough** for idli and dosa is fermented by **bacteria**; the puffed-up appearance is due to **carbon dioxide**.
- **Bread:** dough is fermented by **baker’s yeast, *Saccharomyces cerevisiae***; carbon dioxide makes it rise.
- **Toddy**, a traditional drink of southern India, is made by fermenting **sap from palms**.
- **Cheese:** the large holes in **Swiss cheese** are due to a large amount of **CO₂** produced by the bacterium ***Propionibacterium sharmanii***; **Roquefort cheese** is ripened by growing specific **fungi** on it, which give it a particular flavour.

sections.heading: 2. Microbes in industrial products
sections.body_md:
Microbes are grown on a large scale in very large vessels called **fermentors**.

**Fermented beverages:** ***Saccharomyces cerevisiae*** (**brewer’s yeast**) ferments malted cereals and fruit juices to produce ethanol. **Wine and beer** are produced **without distillation**; **whisky, brandy and rum** are produced by **distillation** of the fermented broth.

**Antibiotics** are chemical substances produced by some microbes that can **kill or retard the growth** of other (disease-causing) microbes. **Penicillin** was the first antibiotic discovered — by **Alexander Fleming**, who saw that a mould, ***Penicillium notatum***, growing in an unwashed culture plate of ***Staphylococcus***, prevented the bacteria from growing around it. Its full potential as an effective antibiotic was established by **Ernst Chain and Howard Florey**; it was used extensively to treat soldiers in **World War II**. Antibiotics have greatly reduced deaths from diseases such as plague, whooping cough, diphtheria and leprosy.

**Chemicals, enzymes and other bioactive molecules:**
| Product | Microbe |
|---|---|
| **Citric acid** | ***Aspergillus niger*** (fungus) |
| **Acetic acid** | ***Acetobacter aceti*** (bacterium) |
| **Butyric acid** | ***Clostridium butylicum*** (bacterium) |
| **Lactic acid** | ***Lactobacillus*** (bacterium) |
| **Ethanol** | ***Saccharomyces cerevisiae*** (yeast) |

- **Lipases** are used in **detergent** formulations to remove **oily stains** from laundry.
- **Pectinases and proteases** make bottled **fruit juices clearer**.
- **Streptokinase**, produced by ***Streptococcus*** and modified by genetic engineering, is a **“clot buster”** that removes clots from blood vessels of patients who have had a **myocardial infarction (heart attack)**.
- **Cyclosporin A**, from the fungus ***Trichoderma polysporum***, is an **immunosuppressive agent** used in **organ-transplant** patients.
- **Statins**, from the yeast ***Monascus purpureus***, are **blood-cholesterol-lowering** agents; they **competitively inhibit** the enzyme responsible for cholesterol synthesis.

key_terms.definition_md: Chemical from a microbe that kills or retards other microbes.
Clot-busting enzyme from Streptococcus.
Immunosuppressant from Trichoderma polysporum.
Cholesterol-lowering agents from Monascus purpureus.

sections.heading: 3. Microbes in sewage treatment
sections.body_md:
**Sewage** is municipal waste water containing large amounts of **organic matter** and microbes, many of them pathogenic. It is treated in **sewage treatment plants (STPs)** in two stages.

**Primary treatment** — physical removal of particles: **floating debris** is removed by **sequential filtration**; **grit** (soil and small pebbles) by **sedimentation**. All solids that settle form the **primary sludge**; the supernatant forms the **effluent**, which goes to secondary treatment.

**Secondary (biological) treatment** — the primary effluent is passed into large **aeration tanks**, where it is constantly agitated and air is pumped in. This allows vigorous growth of useful **aerobic microbes** into **flocs** — masses of **bacteria associated with fungal filaments** forming mesh-like structures. The microbes consume most of the organic matter, **significantly reducing the BOD**.

**BOD (biochemical oxygen demand)** is the amount of **oxygen** that would be consumed if all the **organic matter in one litre of water** were oxidised by bacteria. The greater the BOD, the greater the **polluting potential** (model plant: 360 → 240 → 24 mg/L, a fall of 93.3 percent).

When BOD has fallen enough, the effluent passes into a **settling tank**, where the flocs **sediment** as **activated sludge**. A small part is **pumped back** to the aeration tank as **inoculum**; the major part goes to **anaerobic sludge digesters**, where **anaerobic bacteria** digest the bacteria and fungi, producing gases such as **methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide** — **biogas**. The treated effluent is released into rivers and streams. The Ministry of Environment and Forests began the **Ganga Action Plan** and **Yamuna Action Plan** to build STPs.

key_terms.definition_md: Solids that settle during primary treatment.
Masses of bacteria with fungal filaments that digest organic matter.
Oxygen consumed by bacteria to oxidise the organic matter in one litre of water.

sections.heading: 4. Biogas
sections.body_md:
**Biogas** is a mixture of gases — **predominantly methane**, with **carbon dioxide** and **hydrogen sulphide** — produced by microbial activity and used as **fuel**.

**Methanogens**, such as ***Methanobacterium***, grow **anaerobically on cellulosic material** and produce large amounts of methane along with CO₂ and H₂. They are found in **anaerobic sludge** during sewage treatment and in the **rumen** of cattle, where they help break down the **cellulose** of the cattle’s food. Cattle **excreta (gobar)** are therefore rich in methanogens.

**Biogas plant:** a **concrete tank (10–15 feet deep)** in which bio-wastes are collected and a **slurry of dung** is fed. A **floating cover** is placed over the slurry; it **keeps rising** as gas is produced by microbial activity. The plant has an **outlet** connected to a **pipe** that supplies biogas to nearby houses for **cooking and lighting**. The **spent slurry** is removed through another outlet and used as **fertiliser**. The technology was developed in India mainly by the **Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI)** and the **Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC)**.

sections.heading: 5. Biocontrol agents and integrated pest management
sections.body_md:
**Biocontrol** is the use of **biological methods** for controlling plant diseases and pests. An **organic farmer** holds that **eradicating** pests is undesirable, since predatory and parasitic insects that depend on them would also die; the aim is to keep pests at **manageable levels** through a balanced system.

**Examples:**
- **Ladybird** beetles feed on **aphids**; **dragonflies** feed on **mosquitoes**.
- ***Bacillus thuringiensis* (Bt)**: spores (available in sachets) are mixed with water and sprayed on plants such as brassicas and fruit trees; they are eaten by **caterpillars**, in whose gut the **toxin is released**, killing the larvae without harming other insects.
- ***Trichoderma***: free-living **fungi** common in root ecosystems, effective biocontrol agents against several **plant pathogens**.
- **Baculoviruses** (genus ***Nucleopolyhedrovirus***) attack insects and other arthropods; they are **species-specific** and **narrow-spectrum**, with **no negative impact** on plants, mammals, birds, fish or non-target insects — ideal for **integrated pest management (IPM)** in ecologically sensitive areas.

**Harmful effects of chemical pesticides:** they are **toxic** to humans and animals; they kill **useful and harmful** organisms indiscriminately; they **pollute** soil, water bodies and food (including by **biomagnification** in food chains); and pests develop **resistance**. **IPM** combines biocontrol, resistant varieties, crop rotation and minimal, targeted use of chemicals.

sections.heading: 6. Biofertilisers
sections.body_md:
**Biofertilisers** are organisms that **enrich the nutrient quality of the soil**; the main sources are **bacteria, fungi and cyanobacteria**. They reduce the use of chemical fertilisers.
- ***Rhizobium*** forms **nodules** on the roots of **leguminous** plants and fixes **atmospheric nitrogen** into organic forms usable by the plant (symbiotic).
- ***Azospirillum*** and ***Azotobacter*** are **free-living** bacteria that fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil.
- **Mycorrhiza**: symbiotic associations of fungi, many of the genus ***Glomus***, with plant roots. The fungus **absorbs phosphorus** from the soil and passes it to the plant; mycorrhizal plants also show **resistance to root-borne pathogens**, **tolerance to salinity and drought**, and better growth.
- **Cyanobacteria** (blue-green algae) are **autotrophic** microbes, many of which fix atmospheric nitrogen — for example ***Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria***. In **paddy fields** they are important biofertilisers and also add **organic matter** to the soil.

key_terms.definition_md: Organism that enriches soil nutrients, such as a nitrogen fixer.
Symbiotic association of a fungus with plant roots.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing “Penicillium” as the bacterium in Fleming’s plate (the bacterium was Staphylococcus; the mould was Penicillium notatum).
- Mixing up the sources of cyclosporin A (Trichoderma polysporum) and statins (Monascus purpureus).
- Saying primary treatment is biological (it is physical; secondary is biological).
- Defining BOD as the oxygen in water (it is the oxygen consumed to oxidise the organic matter).
- Saying biogas is mainly carbon dioxide (it is mainly methane).
- Calling Glomus a nitrogen fixer (it helps phosphorus uptake).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a microbe for a product, a gas, a biofertiliser, a use of an enzyme.
- 2–3-mark questions: curd formation; primary vs secondary treatment; BOD; biogas plant; biocontrol examples; biofertilisers.
- 5-mark questions in parts: sewage treatment with diagram; biogas from methanogens to plant; organic farming with biocontrol and biofertilisers.

questions.stem_md: Raw sewage entering a plant has a BOD of 280 mg/L, and the effluent leaving it has a BOD of 21 mg/L. By what percentage has the BOD fallen? (One decimal place.)
Define BOD. Why does untreated sewage with a high BOD kill fish when it is discharged into a river?

answer.model_answer_md: **BOD** is the amount of **oxygen** that would be consumed if all the **organic matter in one litre of water** were oxidised by bacteria. Sewage with high BOD lets bacteria multiply on its organic matter and **use up the dissolved oxygen** of the river, so **fish suffocate**.

marking_scheme.step: Bacteria deplete dissolved oxygen; fish die

questions.stem_md: Describe the primary and secondary treatment of sewage.

answer.model_answer_md: **Primary treatment** is physical: **floating debris** is removed by **sequential filtration** and **grit** by **sedimentation**; settled solids form **primary sludge**, and the **effluent** goes on. **Secondary treatment** is biological: the effluent is **aerated** in large tanks so **aerobic microbes** grow into **flocs** that consume organic matter and **reduce BOD**. The effluent then passes to a **settling tank**, where flocs settle as **activated sludge**.

marking_scheme.step: Secondary: aeration and flocs; BOD falls

questions.stem_md: In a sewage plant, a small part of the activated sludge is pumped back into the aeration tank, while most is pumped into anaerobic sludge digesters. Explain the reason for each step.

answer.model_answer_md: The returned sludge acts as an **inoculum**: it is rich in the **aerobic microbes (flocs)** that digest organic matter, so fresh effluent is treated **quickly**. The rest goes to **anaerobic digesters**, where **anaerobic bacteria** digest the bacteria and fungi in the sludge, reducing its bulk and producing **biogas** (**methane, hydrogen sulphide, carbon dioxide**), which can be used as fuel.

questions.stem_md: BOD was measured at three points along a river: 4 mg/L upstream of a town, 38 mg/L just below an outlet of untreated sewage, and 9 mg/L ten kilometres further downstream. Interpret these values and suggest what the town should do.

answer.model_answer_md: Upstream the water is **clean** (low BOD). Below the outlet the **organic matter** in sewage raises the BOD sharply, so bacteria use up **dissolved oxygen** — harmful to fish. Downstream the BOD falls as **microbes in the river** gradually decompose the organic matter (**self-purification**) and the sewage is **diluted**. The town should build a **sewage treatment plant** so that only treated, low-BOD effluent is released.

questions.stem_md:
(a) With the help of a flow diagram, describe the treatment of sewage in a sewage treatment plant. [3]
(b) What is meant by BOD? [1]
(c) Why is the effluent tested for BOD before it is released into a river? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Raw sewage → primary treatment** (filtration removes floating debris; sedimentation removes grit; **primary sludge** settles) **→ effluent → aeration tank** (aerobic microbes form **flocs** that consume organic matter; BOD falls) **→ settling tank** (flocs settle as **activated sludge**; part returned as **inoculum**, rest to **anaerobic sludge digesters** producing **biogas**) **→ treated effluent** to the river.

(b) **BOD** is the amount of **oxygen consumed** if all the **organic matter in one litre** of water is oxidised by bacteria.

(c) Only if the BOD has fallen enough will the effluent **not deplete** the river’s **dissolved oxygen** and harm aquatic life.

answer.model_answer_md: Pests are part of a **food web**: if they are wiped out, the **predators and parasites** that feed on them, such as **ladybirds** that eat aphids, also disappear, and the **balance** of the ecosystem is lost.
